Band Neutrophil.text: Band neutrophils are associated with a left shift, which indicates an increase in circulating immature granulocytes, often seen in response to infection, inflammation, or stress [2][4]. On a peripheral blood film, bands are characterized by unsegmented nuclear morphology and may be seen alongside other immature forms such as myelocytes and metamyelocytes, especially in severe neutrophilia or leukaemoid reactions [2][4]. Toxic changes like toxic granulation, vacuolation, and Dohle bodies may also be present in neutrophils during such conditions [4].

Basophil.text: Basophils are associated with conditions such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where marked basophilia is a pathognomonic feature and a prognostic factor, and with allergic and inflammatory responses, including COPD and asthma, where tissue infiltration and increased density are observed [2][3][5]. On a peripheral blood film, basophilia may be evident as an increased number of basophils, sometimes quite immature, especially in disease progression or accelerated phases of CML, and may be accompanied by other abnormal cells or features indicating myeloproliferative disorders [6][7].

Eosinophil.text: Eosinophils are associated with a range of conditions, including hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), allergic diseases like asthma and atopic dermatitis, parasitic infections, and certain cancers or drug reactions [1][8]. On a peripheral blood film, eosinophils may be seen in increased numbers, with counts above 0.5×10^9/L indicating eosinophilia and counts ≥1.5×10^9/L indicating hypereosinophilia; their presence can be associated with tissue infiltration and eosinophil granule proteins [2][6][8]. The degree of eosinophilia and associated tissue findings help in diagnosing underlying disorders and assessing disease activity.

Lymphocyte.text: Lymphocytes are associated with reactive processes such as infections and inflammatory conditions, as well as neoplastic lymphoproliferative disorders like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and cutaneous lymphomas [1][4]. On a peripheral blood film, reactive lymphocytes may appear as atypical, pleomorphic, or activated cells, often with abnormal morphology, although phenotypic alterations can occur earlier than morphological changes [2][3]. In CLL, smudge cells are frequently observed, and abnormal lymphocytes may be small and difficult to identify morphologically, especially when phenotypic changes precede morphological alterations [3][4].

Monocyte.text: Monocytes are associated with inflammatory conditions such as atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, infections, and hematologic disorders like myeloproliferative diseases [2][4][7][8]. On a peripheral blood film, monocytosis may be observed as an increased monocyte count, with features such as vacuolation or atypical morphology, which can be associated with initial or milder disease states, including COVID-19 [4][6]. These morphological changes, along with elevated monocyte numbers, support the presence of systemic inflammation or immune response.

Segmented Neutrophil.text: Segmented neutrophils are associated with sepsis and severe infections, often showing morphological abnormalities such as toxic granulations, vacuolar degeneration, and hypersegmentation [4][8]. In cases of severe infection, a leukaemoid reaction with toxic granulations may be observed, indicating increased microbicidal activity. Additionally, neutrophil hypersegmentation can be seen in megaloblastic anemia, characterized by neutrophils with six or more nuclear segments [8].

Monocyte|vacuolated.text: Monocytes are associated with inflammatory conditions such as monocytosis in acute and chronic inflammation, including atherosclerosis, and can be part of clonal disorders like CMML [5][6]. On peripheral blood films, monocytes typically show variable nuclear shapes, a ground glass blue-gray cytoplasm with fine granules, and may have pseudopods or vacuoles [1]. Cytoplasmic vacuolation in monocytes can be associated with reactive or infectious states, and in COVID-19, it has been linked to milder disease and shorter hospital stays [4].

Segmented Neutrophil|vacuolated.text: Segmented neutrophils are associated with conditions such as sepsis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and septic shock, where morphological changes like toxic granulation, Dohle bodies, and vacuolation are observed [1][8]. On peripheral blood films, these cells may show toxic granules, cytoplasmic vacuolation, and Dohle bodies, indicating activation and toxicity [8]. Cytoplasmic vacuolation suggests phagocytic activity, autophagocytosis, or cellular response to infection or inflammation [8].
